11: # Epic E1.1 — Foundation Decisions and Working Baseline
12: 
13: ## Context
14: 
15: P1-M1 is being delivered as Attempt 2 under Creation Chat Steering Note SN-2
16: (`.ai-project/artifacts/steering-notes/2026-09-05__creation-chat__steering-note__P1-M1-restart.md`).
17: Attempt 1 produced rejected Epic deliveries and recovery churn without ever
18: producing an application baseline. Its decisions are frozen under
19: `archive/P1-M1-attempt-1/*` and are not accepted authority; every active choice
20: in this Epic must be freshly selected against current requirements and current
21: primary evidence.
22: 
23: This Epic performs the first half of the M1 foundation work: it resolves and
24: records the four application-level foundation decisions that precede all code,
25: then builds the minimum runnable application baseline that demonstrates those
26: choices. It deliberately stops short of M2 public-experience work and M3
27: LLM/chat behavior. The companion Epic P1-M1-E1.2 owns hosting, deployment, and
28: domain decisions and consumes the decisions made here.
29: 
30: ## Problem Statement
31: 
32: M2 and M3 cannot start until the application foundation is fixed and
33: demonstrable. Attempt 1 left no accepted framework, architecture, data, or
34: LLM-provider-choice record, and no runnable baseline, so every downstream step
35: inherits unresolved choices. Without this Epic:
36: 
37: - There is no agreed framework/language, architecture, or data boundary for M2
38:   to build on.
39: - There is no runnable artifact proving the chosen stack builds, runs, and passes
40:   checks from a clean checkout.
41: - There is no LLM-provider constraint record, so M3 cannot be scoped against a
42:   foundation even though M3 itself is deferred.
43: - There is no executable performance budget, so M2/M3 have no baseline bar.
44: 
45: ## Goals
46: 
47: By the end of this Epic, the project must:
48: 
49: 1. Have four committed decision records — application framework and language,
50:    application architecture, data services and persistence boundaries, and
51:    LLM-provider foundation constraints — each standalone and consumable by E1.2,
52:    M2, and M3 without an archived Attempt 1 dependency. (The executor commits
53:    and submits them; acceptance is the parent's decision after review.)
54: 2. Have a minimum application baseline that installs, builds, starts, and exposes
55:    only public-safe non-LLM baseline behavior (health, revision, and the minimal
56:    status page), with no M2
57:    experience or M3 LLM/chat functionality.
58: 3. Have reproducible, pinned local commands for install, build, start, test, and
59:    the performance budget.
60: 4. Have proportionate automated checks covering correctness, accessibility,
61:    security, and performance, each naming a reproducible tool, its pinning
62:    method, tested scope, exact assertions or rules, thresholds, expected results,
63:    and fail-closed behavior.
64: 5. Leave E1.2, M2, and M3 with explicit, consistent foundation contracts rather
65:    than unresolved implementation choices.
66: 
67: ## Non-Goals
68: 
69: This Epic explicitly does **not** aim to:
70: 
71: - Build any M2 public-experience, homepage, CV, or scheduling surface.
72: - Implement any M3 LLM call, chat UI, retrieval, citation, or evidence processing.
73: - Select or configure a deployment platform, repository-hosting workflow, or
74:   production-domain path (owned by P1-M1-E1.2).
75: - Perform any real deployment, repository-setting change, credential action,
76:   domain purchase, DNS change, or certificate action.
77: - Import or revive any Attempt 1 decision, recovery contract, or provenance
78:   machinery.
79: - Upgrade or modify the pinned `.governance/` dependency, the M1 spec, Phase
80:   artifacts, or any M2/M3 artifact.
81: 
82: ## Decision Gates (execute before dependent code)
83: 
84: This Epic owns four of the seven M1 decision gates. Each must be recorded as a
85: standalone, immutable decision under `docs/decisions/` **before** the dependent
86: baseline implementation begins, and each record must:
87: 
88: - Be standalone: consumable without reference to any archived Attempt 1
89:   artifact.
90: - Cite **current primary evidence** for every material technical claim (for
91:   example, framework/language LTS and security-support status from the
92:   maintainer; dependency management and lockfile behavior from the tool's own
93:   documentation; data-store licensing and maintenance status from the vendor).
94: - Define prerequisites and owner for the choice.
95: - State concrete effects on the other M1 Epic (P1-M1-E1.2) and on downstream
96:   M2/M3 work.
97: 
98: ### D1 — Application framework and language
99: 
100: Select the framework and language used to implement the baseline and the M2/M3
101: experience. The decision must name the language and runtime version, the web
102: framework, and the method used to pin the runtime and dependencies for
103: reproducible builds.
104: 
105: **Requirements:**
106: 
107: - Must support a fast first paint, accessible focus states, keyboard-operable
108:   surfaces, and strong mobile behavior, since these are binding P1 constraints
109:   inherited by M2/M3.
110: - Must be reproducible from a clean checkout using pinned tooling (for example a
111:   runtime version file and a lockfile), with no version drift on reinstall.
112: - Must explicitly note any implication for the E1.2 deployment platform (static
113:   vs. serverful runtime, build output shape) even though E1.2 makes the platform
114:   decision.
115: 
116: ### D2 — Application architecture
117: 
118: Select the application architecture, covering component boundaries, the
119: serving/rendering model, and the routing surface for the baseline and the future
120: M2/M3 features.
121: 
122: **Requirements:**
123: 
124: - Must permit the selected non-LLM baseline routes (health, revision, and the
125:   minimal `GET /` status page) as the only live behavior in M1.
126: - Must prohibit M3 LLM/chat/retrieval/provider behavior in M1 and M2.
127: - Must name where M2 experience routes and M3 chatbot/retrieval routes will later
128:   attach without re-architecting the foundation.
129: - Must keep deployment-target assumptions (from D1) consistent with what E1.2
130:   will consume.
131: 
132: ### D3 — Data services and application-persistence boundaries
133: 
134: Select the data services used by the baseline and the persistence boundary that
135: M2 and M3 will inherit, or explicitly record that the baseline requires no
136: persistent data store and where persistence will be introduced later.
137: 
138: **Requirements:**
139: 
140: - Must define the application-persistence boundary precisely enough that M2 and
141:   M3 consume it without an archived dependency.
142: - Must state whether any data service is part of the M1 baseline and, if so, its
143:   version and provisioning boundaries; the baseline must run without any
144:   external data service that is not explicitly required by this decision.
145: - Must note any licensing, cost, or provider-state implication for E1.2's
146:   deployment boundary (but must not select or configure deployment itself).
147: 
148: ### D4 — LLM-provider foundation constraints
149: 
150: Record the LLM-provider constraints that affect the foundation, while deferring
151: all LLM, chat, retrieval, prompt, and provider-integration behavior to M3.
152: 
153: **Requirements:**
154: 
155: - Must name the class of LLM provider/API the foundation must accommodate (for
156:   example, a hosted API requiring a server-side secret) without selecting a
157:   specific vendor, account, or key.
158: - Must define the secret and network boundary that the foundation reserves for
159:   M3 so that no M1 or M2 route can reach an LLM.
160: - Must explicitly prohibit any M3 behavior from appearing in M1 or M2.
161: 
162: ## Scope of Work
163: 
164: ### 1. Foundation decision records
165: 
166: Produce the four decision records above under `docs/decisions/`, each with the
167: front-matter required by PSG §5 and a `type: decision` status. Each record stands
168: alone, cites current primary evidence, and states effects on E1.2/M2/M3.
169: 
170: **Must include:**
171: 
172: - A decision record for each of D1, D2, D3, and D4.
173: - Standalone readability with no `archive/` reference as a dependency.
174: - Current primary evidence citations for every material claim.
175: - Prerequisites and owner for each choice.
176: 
177: ### 2. Minimum application baseline
178: 
179: Implement the smallest runnable application that demonstrates D1–D3 and the D4
180: prohibition.
181: 
182: **Must include:**
183: 
184: - A clean-checkout install, build, and start path using the pinned tooling from D1.
185: - Exactly three public-safe non-LLM routes:
186:   - `GET /health` → `200`, `Content-Type: application/json`, body
187:     `{"status":"ok"}` and nothing else.
188:   - `GET /revision` → `200`, `Content-Type: application/json`, body
189:     `{"revision":"<public-safe build/revision label>"}` where the label is a
190:     public-safe identifier (for example a short commit hash or version string)
191:     and exposes no secrets, absolute paths, or environment details.
192:   - `GET /` → `200`, `Content-Type: text/html`, a minimal accessible HTML
193:     document containing `<html lang="en">`, a `<head>` with a `<title>`, a single
194:     `<main>` landmark, at least one focusable element, and visible revision text.
195:     It must remain minimal and must not be the M2 homepage.
196:   - Any other route returns `404`.
197: - No M2 experience routes and no M3 LLM/chat/retrieval/provider behavior.
198: 
199: ### 3. Reproducible local commands and pinned tooling
200: 
201: Pin every tool and dependency used to install, build, start, test, and
202: performance-check the baseline.
203: 
204: **Must include:**
205: 
206: - A declarative, committed pinning mechanism (lockfile and/or runtime version
207:   file) that produces identical resolution on reinstall.
208: - Documented commands for install, build, start, test, and performance check.
209: - A statement of expected results for each command on a clean checkout.
210: 
211: ### 4. Proportionate automated checks
212: 
213: Add automated checks that enforce a correctness, accessibility, security, and
214: performance baseline. Each must name a reproducible tool, its pinning method,
215: tested scope, exact assertions or rules, thresholds, expected results, and
216: fail-closed behavior. The tool identity and its exact pinned version are locked
217: to the D1-selected stack at execution; the rule sets, thresholds, and fail-closed
218: behavior below are fixed by this contract and are not open to deferral.
219: 
220: **Must include:**
221: 
222: - **Correctness.** The D1 stack's default test runner, pinned via the lockfile.
223:   Scope: the baseline routes. Assertions, exactly:
224:   - `GET /health` returns `200`, `Content-Type: application/json`, body
225:     `{"status":"ok"}`.
226:   - `GET /revision` returns `200`, `Content-Type: application/json`, body with a
227:     single `revision` string field.
228:   - `GET /` returns `200`, `Content-Type: text/html`, and the document contains
229:     `<html lang="en">`, a `<title>`, a `<main>` landmark, and at least one
230:     focusable element.
231:   - Any other route returns `404`.
232:   Expected result: all pass. Fail closed: any failure produces a non-zero exit.
233: - **Accessibility.** axe-core (or the D1 stack's equivalent engine) pinned via the
234:   lockfile. Target: the single HTML document the baseline serves at `GET /` (the
235:   concrete target that makes this check non-vacuous). The check MUST run against
236:   that served document and MUST fail closed if no HTML rule actually evaluated
237:   (a zero-target guard). Rules: WCAG 2.2 AA automated ruleset, including the
238:   document-title, html-lang, and landmark (main) rules. Threshold: zero
239:   violations. Expected result: no violations. Fail closed: any violation, or a
240:   zero-target run, produces a non-zero exit in the accessibility-check command.
241: - **Security.** Two parts, both fail closed (non-zero exit):
242:   - Dependency scan: the selected ecosystem's pinned audit tool, failing on any
243:     advisory at `high` or `critical` severity. Threshold: zero findings at/above
244:     `high`. Expected result: clean.
245:   - Secret hygiene: a deterministic, bounded assertion over `GET /health`,
246:     `GET /revision`, and `GET /`, executed in a sanitized environment so results
247:     never depend on ambient values (no value-content matching of benign strings):
248:     1. Sanitized environment + canary injection: before the run, the check
249:        unsets every environment variable whose name matches the secret-name
250:        rule `(_KEY|_SECRET|_TOKEN|_PASSWORD|_API_KEY|_CREDENTIAL)$`
251:        (case-insensitive suffix), then injects exactly two canary variables
252:        (`PANCHEW_CANARY_API_KEY`, `PANCHEW_CANARY_SECRET`) with fixed non-empty
253:        collision-free 40-hex values. No ambient secret-named value remains to
254:        compare against.
255:     2. `GET /health` body is exactly the single-key object `{"status":"ok"}`;
256:        `GET /revision` body is exactly the single-key object
257:        `{"revision":"<label>"}` — no additional keys.
258:     3. Across all three responses (`/health`, `/revision`, `/`): neither canary
259:        value appears. No absolute filesystem path or path-like token appears,
260:        using these exact patterns (which do not match HTML closing tags):
261:        - Unix absolute path (two or more segments), with a leading `/` not
262:          immediately preceded by `<`:
263:          `/([A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)(/[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)+`;
264:        - Windows drive path: `\b[A-Za-z]:[\\/]`;
265:        - Home path: `~/([A-Za-z0-9_.-]+/)*[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+`.
266:     4. The `status` and `revision` values match `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$` only; the
267:        `GET /` HTML document's visible text is limited to its title and the
268:        revision label.
269:     Threshold: zero rule violations. Expected result: clean.
270: - **Performance.** An executable, protocol-fixed budget using a pinned HTTP load
271:   tool (the D1 stack's equivalent of auto-cannon), pinned via the lockfile.
272:   Protocol (fixed, not executor-chosen):
273:   - Response validation (warm-up and sustained requests only): each such request
274:     must return the expected status and content type for its route (`/health`
275:     and `/revision` → `200` + `application/json`; `/` → `200` + `text/html`).
276:     Any unexpected status or content type counts as a request error; the error
277:     count across warm-up and sustained requests must be zero.
278:   - Per-request timeout (warm-up and sustained requests): 5,000 ms; any request
279:     exceeding it counts as an error.
280:   - Warm-up: after start, send 100 warm-up requests per route before recording;
281:     warm-up requests are excluded from latency results but still subject to the
282:     zero-error validation above.
283:   - Sustained window: 1,000 requests per route at 10 concurrent connections;
284:     metric is the tool's 95th-percentile response latency (p95) over that window;
285:     zero request errors in the window.
286:   - Cold start: measured once per run in a separate cold process (no warm-up),
287:     using a monotonic clock from process launch until the first `GET /health`
288:     `200`, probing `GET /health` at a fixed 100 ms cadence. Probe failures before
289:     the first successful `200` are expected and are not counted as errors; the
290:     run fails closed only if no `200` is observed within the 10 s cold-start
291:     threshold.
292:   - Host assumptions: measurement is local-only and network-free (the baseline
293:     makes no external calls during measurement); the Delivery Notice must record
294:     the runtime version, OS, and architecture used for the run.
295:   Thresholds: sustained p95 ≤ 100 ms per route; cold start ≤ 10 s; zero request
296:   errors. Failure behavior: the benchmark command exits non-zero if any
297:   threshold is exceeded (including any request error) or the protocol could not
298:   be executed as specified.
299: 
300: ## Deliverables
301: 
302: This Epic must produce:
303: 
304: - [ ] Four committed decision records under `docs/decisions/` (D1–D4), submitted for parent acceptance.
305: - [ ] The minimum application baseline committed to the repository.
306: - [ ] Pinned dependency/runtime configuration and lockfiles.
307: - [ ] Documented, reproducible install/build/start/test/performance commands.
308: - [ ] Automated correctness, accessibility, security, and performance checks per §Scope of Work item 4.
309: - [ ] One standard pre-review Delivery Notice (schema per artifact-communication-protocol §1).
310: - [ ] A proposed structural visual in this spec and an implemented structural visual in the Delivery Notice.
311: 
312: ## Definition of Done
313: 
314: Epic E1.1 is complete when:
315: 
316: - [ ] D1, D2, D3, and D4 are recorded as standalone decisions and committed before dependent code.
317: - [ ] Each decision cites current primary evidence and states effects on E1.2/M2/M3.
318: - [ ] The baseline installs, builds, and starts from a clean checkout using pinned tooling.
319: - [ ] The baseline exposes only the specified public-safe routes (`GET /health`, `GET /revision`, `GET /`) and contains no M2 or M3 functionality.
320: - [ ] Correctness, accessibility, security, and performance checks pass and fail closed exactly as specified in §Scope of Work item 4.
321: - [ ] The implemented structural visual is recorded.
322: - [ ] All changes are committed to `epic/E1.1` and the working tree is clean.
323: - [ ] One standard pre-review Delivery Notice is produced and committed.
324: 
325: ## Acceptance Criteria
326: 
327: - [ ] A reviewer can recreate the project state from a clean checkout and run the documented install, build, start, test, accessibility, security, and performance commands with the documented expected results.
328: - [ ] The running baseline answers `GET /health`, `GET /revision`, and `GET /` with the exact specified status, content type, and body, and reveals no secrets, paths, or environment details.
329: - [ ] The four decision records are readable standalone and contain no unresolved foundation choice delegated to M2 or M3.
330: - [ ] E1.2, M2, and M3 can each consume the committed decisions without reading an archived Attempt 1 artifact.
331: - [ ] No M2 experience or M3 LLM/chat behavior exists anywhere in the delivered baseline.
332: 
333: ## Technical Constraints
334: 
335: **Format:** Markdown with YAML front-matter (PSG §5) for decisions and specs.
336: **Technology:** The framework/language is selected by D1 during execution, not pre-set here; every selected tool must be pinned to a reproducible version.

343: - Parent Milestone P1-M1 spec and this Epic's accepted starter.

353: 
354: This Epic performs **no external mutation and no application/provider call**.
355: Prohibited without separate parent authorization: deployment, repository-setting

367:

# Epic E1.1 — Foundation Decisions and Working Baseline

## Context

P1-M1 is being delivered as Attempt 2 under Creation Chat Steering Note SN-2
(`.ai-project/artifacts/steering-notes/2026-09-05__creation-chat__steering-note__P1-M1-restart.md`).
Attempt 1 produced rejected Epic deliveries and recovery churn without ever
producing an application baseline. Its decisions are frozen under
`archive/P1-M1-attempt-1/*` and are not accepted authority; every active choice
in this Epic must be freshly selected against current requirements and current
primary evidence.

This Epic performs the first half of the M1 foundation work: it resolves and
records the four application-level foundation decisions that precede all code,
then builds the minimum runnable application baseline that demonstrates those
choices. It deliberately stops short of M2 public-experience work and M3
LLM/chat behavior. The companion Epic P1-M1-E1.2 owns hosting, deployment, and
domain decisions and consumes the decisions made here.

## Problem Statement

M2 and M3 cannot start until the application foundation is fixed and
demonstrable. Attempt 1 left no accepted framework, architecture, data, or
LLM-provider-choice record, and no runnable baseline, so every downstream step
inherits unresolved choices. Without this Epic:

- There is no agreed framework/language, architecture, or data boundary for M2
  to build on.
- There is no runnable artifact proving the chosen stack builds, runs, and passes
  checks from a clean checkout.
- There is no LLM-provider constraint record, so M3 cannot be scoped against a
  foundation even though M3 itself is deferred.
- There is no executable performance budget, so M2/M3 have no baseline bar.

## Goals

By the end of this Epic, the project must:

1. Have four committed decision records — application framework and language,
   application architecture, data services and persistence boundaries, and
   LLM-provider foundation constraints — each standalone and consumable by E1.2,
   M2, and M3 without an archived Attempt 1 dependency. (The executor commits
   and submits them; acceptance is the parent's decision after review.)
2. Have a minimum application baseline that installs, builds, starts, and exposes
   only public-safe non-LLM baseline behavior (health, revision, and the minimal
   status page), with no M2
   experience or M3 LLM/chat functionality.
3. Have reproducible, pinned local commands for install, build, start, test, and
   the performance budget.
4. Have proportionate automated checks covering correctness, accessibility,
   security, and performance, each naming a reproducible tool, its pinning
   method, tested scope, exact assertions or rules, thresholds, expected results,
   and fail-closed behavior.
5. Leave E1.2, M2, and M3 with explicit, consistent foundation contracts rather
   than unresolved implementation choices.

## Non-Goals

This Epic explicitly does **not** aim to:

- Build any M2 public-experience, homepage, CV, or scheduling surface.
- Implement any M3 LLM call, chat UI, retrieval, citation, or evidence processing.
- Select or configure a deployment platform, repository-hosting workflow, or
  production-domain path (owned by P1-M1-E1.2).
- Perform any real deployment, repository-setting change, credential action,
  domain purchase, DNS change, or certificate action.
- Import or revive any Attempt 1 decision, recovery contract, or provenance
  machinery.
- Upgrade or modify the pinned `.governance/` dependency, the M1 spec, Phase
  artifacts, or any M2/M3 artifact.

## Decision Gates (execute before dependent code)

This Epic owns four of the seven M1 decision gates. Each must be recorded as a
standalone, immutable decision under `docs/decisions/` **before** the dependent
baseline implementation begins, and each record must:

- Be standalone: consumable without reference to any archived Attempt 1
  artifact.
- Cite **current primary evidence** for every material technical claim (for
  example, framework/language LTS and security-support status from the
  maintainer; dependency management and lockfile behavior from the tool's own
  documentation; data-store licensing and maintenance status from the vendor).
- Define prerequisites and owner for the choice.
- State concrete effects on the other M1 Epic (P1-M1-E1.2) and on downstream
  M2/M3 work.

### D1 — Application framework and language

Select the framework and language used to implement the baseline and the M2/M3
experience. The decision must name the language and runtime version, the web
framework, and the method used to pin the runtime and dependencies for
reproducible builds.

**Requirements:**

- Must support a fast first paint, accessible focus states, keyboard-operable
  surfaces, and strong mobile behavior, since these are binding P1 constraints
  inherited by M2/M3.
- Must be reproducible from a clean checkout using pinned tooling (for example a
  runtime version file and a lockfile), with no version drift on reinstall.
- Must explicitly note any implication for the E1.2 deployment platform (static
  vs. serverful runtime, build output shape) even though E1.2 makes the platform
  decision.

### D2 — Application architecture

Select the application architecture, covering component boundaries, the
serving/rendering model, and the routing surface for the baseline and the future
M2/M3 features.

**Requirements:**

- Must permit the selected non-LLM baseline routes (health, revision, and the
  minimal `GET /` status page) as the only live behavior in M1.
- Must prohibit M3 LLM/chat/retrieval/provider behavior in M1 and M2.
- Must name where M2 experience routes and M3 chatbot/retrieval routes will later
  attach without re-architecting the foundation.
- Must keep deployment-target assumptions (from D1) consistent with what E1.2
  will consume.

### D3 — Data services and application-persistence boundaries

Select the data services used by the baseline and the persistence boundary that
M2 and M3 will inherit, or explicitly record that the baseline requires no
persistent data store and where persistence will be introduced later.

**Requirements:**

- Must define the application-persistence boundary precisely enough that M2 and
  M3 consume it without an archived dependency.
- Must state whether any data service is part of the M1 baseline and, if so, its
  version and provisioning boundaries; the baseline must run without any
  external data service that is not explicitly required by this decision.
- Must note any licensing, cost, or provider-state implication for E1.2's
  deployment boundary (but must not select or configure deployment itself).

### D4 — LLM-provider foundation constraints

Record the LLM-provider constraints that affect the foundation, while deferring
all LLM, chat, retrieval, prompt, and provider-integration behavior to M3.

**Requirements:**

- Must name the class of LLM provider/API the foundation must accommodate (for
  example, a hosted API requiring a server-side secret) without selecting a
  specific vendor, account, or key.
- Must define the secret and network boundary that the foundation reserves for
  M3 so that no M1 or M2 route can reach an LLM.
- Must explicitly prohibit any M3 behavior from appearing in M1 or M2.

## Scope of Work

### 1. Foundation decision records

Produce the four decision records above under `docs/decisions/`, each with the
front-matter required by PSG §5 and a `type: decision` status. Each record stands
alone, cites current primary evidence, and states effects on E1.2/M2/M3.

**Must include:**

- A decision record for each of D1, D2, D3, and D4.
- Standalone readability with no `archive/` reference as a dependency.
- Current primary evidence citations for every material claim.
- Prerequisites and owner for each choice.

### 2. Minimum application baseline

Implement the smallest runnable application that demonstrates D1–D3 and the D4
prohibition.

**Must include:**

- A clean-checkout install, build, and start path using the pinned tooling from D1.
- Exactly three public-safe non-LLM routes:
  - `GET /health` → `200`, `Content-Type: application/json`, body
    `{"status":"ok"}` and nothing else.
  - `GET /revision` → `200`, `Content-Type: application/json`, body
    `{"revision":"<public-safe build/revision label>"}` where the label is a
    public-safe identifier (for example a short commit hash or version string)
    and exposes no secrets, absolute paths, or environment details.
  - `GET /` → `200`, `Content-Type: text/html`, a minimal accessible HTML
    document containing `<html lang="en">`, a `<head>` with a `<title>`, a single
    `<main>` landmark, at least one focusable element, and visible revision text.
    It must remain minimal and must not be the M2 homepage.
  - Any other route returns `404`.
- No M2 experience routes and no M3 LLM/chat/retrieval/provider behavior.

### 3. Reproducible local commands and pinned tooling

Pin every tool and dependency used to install, build, start, test, and
performance-check the baseline.

**Must include:**

- A declarative, committed pinning mechanism (lockfile and/or runtime version
  file) that produces identical resolution on reinstall.
- Documented commands for install, build, start, test, and performance check.
- A statement of expected results for each command on a clean checkout.

### 4. Proportionate automated checks

Add automated checks that enforce a correctness, accessibility, security, and
performance baseline. Each must name a reproducible tool, its pinning method,
tested scope, exact assertions or rules, thresholds, expected results, and
fail-closed behavior. The tool identity and its exact pinned version are locked
to the D1-selected stack at execution; the rule sets, thresholds, and fail-closed
behavior below are fixed by this contract and are not open to deferral.

**Must include:**

- **Correctness.** The D1 stack's default test runner, pinned via the lockfile.
  Scope: the baseline routes. Assertions, exactly:
  - `GET /health` returns `200`, `Content-Type: application/json`, body
    `{"status":"ok"}`.
  - `GET /revision` returns `200`, `Content-Type: application/json`, body with a
    single `revision` string field.
  - `GET /` returns `200`, `Content-Type: text/html`, and the document contains
    `<html lang="en">`, a `<title>`, a `<main>` landmark, and at least one
    focusable element.
  - Any other route returns `404`.
  Expected result: all pass. Fail closed: any failure produces a non-zero exit.
- **Accessibility.** axe-core (or the D1 stack's equivalent engine) pinned via the
  lockfile. Target: the single HTML document the baseline serves at `GET /` (the
  concrete target that makes this check non-vacuous). The check MUST run against
  that served document and MUST fail closed if no HTML rule actually evaluated
  (a zero-target guard). Rules: WCAG 2.2 AA automated ruleset, including the
  document-title, html-lang, and landmark (main) rules. Threshold: zero
  violations. Expected result: no violations. Fail closed: any violation, or a
  zero-target run, produces a non-zero exit in the accessibility-check command.
- **Security.** Two parts, both fail closed (non-zero exit):
  - Dependency scan: the selected ecosystem's pinned audit tool, failing on any
    advisory at `high` or `critical` severity. Threshold: zero findings at/above
    `high`. Expected result: clean.
  - Secret hygiene: a deterministic, bounded assertion over `GET /health`,
    `GET /revision`, and `GET /`, executed in a sanitized environment so results
    never depend on ambient values (no value-content matching of benign strings):
    1. Sanitized environment + canary injection: before the run, the check
       unsets every environment variable whose name matches the secret-name
       rule `(_KEY|_SECRET|_TOKEN|_PASSWORD|_API_KEY|_CREDENTIAL)$`
       (case-insensitive suffix), then injects exactly two canary variables
       (`PANCHEW_CANARY_API_KEY`, `PANCHEW_CANARY_SECRET`) with fixed non-empty
       collision-free 40-hex values. No ambient secret-named value remains to
       compare against.
    2. `GET /health` body is exactly the single-key object `{"status":"ok"}`;
       `GET /revision` body is exactly the single-key object
       `{"revision":"<label>"}` — no additional keys.
    3. Across all three responses (`/health`, `/revision`, `/`): neither canary
       value appears. No absolute filesystem path or path-like token appears,
       using these exact patterns (which do not match HTML closing tags):
       - Unix absolute path (two or more segments), with a leading `/` not
         immediately preceded by `<`:
         `/([A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)(/[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)+`;
       - Windows drive path: `\b[A-Za-z]:[\\/]`;
       - Home path: `~/([A-Za-z0-9_.-]+/)*[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+`.
    4. The `status` and `revision` values match `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$` only; the
       `GET /` HTML document's visible text is limited to its title and the
       revision label.
    Threshold: zero rule violations. Expected result: clean.
- **Performance.** An executable, protocol-fixed budget using a pinned HTTP load
  tool (the D1 stack's equivalent of auto-cannon), pinned via the lockfile.
  Protocol (fixed, not executor-chosen):
  - Response validation (warm-up and sustained requests only): each such request
    must return the expected status and content type for its route (`/health`
    and `/revision` → `200` + `application/json`; `/` → `200` + `text/html`).
    Any unexpected status or content type counts as a request error; the error
    count across warm-up and sustained requests must be zero.
  - Per-request timeout (warm-up and sustained requests): 5,000 ms; any request
    exceeding it counts as an error.
  - Warm-up: after start, send 100 warm-up requests per route before recording;
    warm-up requests are excluded from latency results but still subject to the
    zero-error validation above.
  - Sustained window: 1,000 requests per route at 10 concurrent connections;
    metric is the tool's 95th-percentile response latency (p95) over that window;
    zero request errors in the window.
  - Cold start: measured once per run in a separate cold process (no warm-up),
    using a monotonic clock from process launch until the first `GET /health`
    `200`, probing `GET /health` at a fixed 100 ms cadence. Probe failures before
    the first successful `200` are expected and are not counted as errors; the
    run fails closed only if no `200` is observed within the 10 s cold-start
    threshold.
  - Host assumptions: measurement is local-only and network-free (the baseline
    makes no external calls during measurement); the Delivery Notice must record
    the runtime version, OS, and architecture used for the run.
  Thresholds: sustained p95 ≤ 100 ms per route; cold start ≤ 10 s; zero request
  errors. Failure behavior: the benchmark command exits non-zero if any
  threshold is exceeded (including any request error) or the protocol could not
  be executed as specified.

## Deliverables

This Epic must produce:

- [ ] Four committed decision records under `docs/decisions/` (D1–D4), submitted for parent acceptance.
- [ ] The minimum application baseline committed to the repository.
- [ ] Pinned dependency/runtime configuration and lockfiles.
- [ ] Documented, reproducible install/build/start/test/performance commands.
- [ ] Automated correctness, accessibility, security, and performance checks per §Scope of Work item 4.
- [ ] One standard pre-review Delivery Notice (schema per artifact-communication-protocol §1).
- [ ] A proposed structural visual in this spec and an implemented structural visual in the Delivery Notice.

## Definition of Done

Epic E1.1 is complete when:

- [ ] D1, D2, D3, and D4 are recorded as standalone decisions and committed before dependent code.
- [ ] Each decision cites current primary evidence and states effects on E1.2/M2/M3.
- [ ] The baseline installs, builds, and starts from a clean checkout using pinned tooling.
- [ ] The baseline exposes only the specified public-safe routes (`GET /health`, `GET /revision`, `GET /`) and contains no M2 or M3 functionality.
- [ ] Correctness, accessibility, security, and performance checks pass and fail closed exactly as specified in §Scope of Work item 4.
- [ ] The implemented structural visual is recorded.
- [ ] All changes are committed to `epic/E1.1` and the working tree is clean.
- [ ] One standard pre-review Delivery Notice is produced and committed.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A reviewer can recreate the project state from a clean checkout and run the documented install, build, start, test, accessibility, security, and performance commands with the documented expected results.
- [ ] The running baseline answers `GET /health`, `GET /revision`, and `GET /` with the exact specified status, content type, and body, and reveals no secrets, paths, or environment details.
- [ ] The four decision records are readable standalone and contain no unresolved foundation choice delegated to M2 or M3.
- [ ] E1.2, M2, and M3 can each consume the committed decisions without reading an archived Attempt 1 artifact.
- [ ] No M2 experience or M3 LLM/chat behavior exists anywhere in the delivered baseline.

## Technical Constraints

**Format:** Markdown with YAML front-matter (PSG §5) for decisions and specs.
**Technology:** The framework/language is selected by D1 during execution, not pre-set here; every selected tool must be pinned to a reproducible version.
**Reproducibility:** Clean-checkout install and build must not drift across runs; lockfiles and runtime version files are committed.
**Boundary:** No LLM/chat/retrieval/provider behavior; no M2 experience routes; no secrets or non-public identifiers in the public surface.

## Dependencies

**Internal Dependencies:**
- Parent Milestone P1-M1 spec and this Epic's accepted starter.
- P1-M1-E1.2 is planned after Phase P1 accepts this planning set; P1-M1-E1.2 executes only after E1.1 is accepted and merged (see E1.2 planning for its own sequencing).

**External Dependencies:**
- None for execution; deployment-provider and domain state are out of scope for E1.1.

**Blockers:**
- None known. If any required primary evidence is unavailable, execution must stop and escalate.

## External-Action Gates

This Epic performs **no external mutation and no application/provider call**.
Prohibited without separate parent authorization: deployment, repository-setting
changes, credential creation, domain purchase, DNS changes, certificate actions,
any application or LLM/data-service provider call, and any PR creation or merge.

Permitted without authorization, since they are read-only or build-necessary:
retrieval of current primary evidence from public documentation for decision
research, and package-registry access during pinned dependency installation.

No external mutation, provider call, PR, or production change occurs without
separate parent authorization.

## Verification Commands

The following commands must exist and be documented with their expected results;
the tool identity and pinned version are locked to the D1-selected stack during
execution, while the assertions and thresholds are fixed by §Scope of Work item 4:

- **Install:** `install` — resolves and installs pinned dependencies; expected: lockfile-identical resolution, zero errors.
- **Build:** `build` — produces the runnable baseline artifact; expected: clean exit, artifact present.
- **Start:** `start` — starts the baseline; expected: `GET /health`, `GET /revision`, and `GET /` respond as specified.
- **Test (correctness):** `test` — runs the pinned test suite; expected: all §4 assertions pass, non-zero exit on any failure.
- **Accessibility:** `check:a11y` — runs the WCAG 2.2 AA rules over served HTML; expected: zero violations, else non-zero exit.
- **Security:** `audit:security` — runs the dependency scan at the `high` severity gate plus the secret-hygiene assertion; expected: zero findings/matches, else non-zero exit.
- **Performance:** `bench:perf` — runs the executable budget; expected: p95 ≤ 100 ms per route and cold start ≤ 10 s, else non-zero exit.

## Delivery Notice

On completion, the Epic produces exactly **one** pre-review Delivery Notice at
`docs/phases/P1__Alpha_Platform_Launch/P1-M1-E1.1__delivery-notice.md`, following
the schema in `artifact-communication-protocol.md` §1 (`status: ready_for_review`;
`pr_details.number: pending`, `pr_details.url: not_created_yet`, since no PR is
created before review). It records what was delivered, verified, and deferred,

append-only and must not modify this spec. PR creation and merge are separate,

choices while producing a working application baseline, then establishes the
private GitHub workflow and proves a repeatable deployment foundation.

## Restart Boundary

This is P1-M1 Attempt 2 under Creation Chat Steering Note SN-2 at
`.ai-project/artifacts/steering-notes/2026-09-05__creation-chat__steering-note__P1-M1-restart.md`.

Attempt 1 is frozen under `archive/P1-M1-attempt-1/*`. Its decisions and delivery
artifacts are not accepted authority and may be consulted only as research leads.
Every Attempt 2 choice must be selected against current requirements and current
authoritative evidence. No Attempt 1 recovery contract, replacement-Epic chain,
or custom provenance machinery may be revived.

## Goals

1. Record all seven M1 foundation decisions with clear constraints, tradeoffs,
   selected directions, evidence, and downstream effects.
2. Produce a runnable application baseline that demonstrates the selected stack
   and architecture without implementing M2 or M3 product features.
3. Establish and verify the delivery workflow for the existing private
   `panchew/panchew-io` GitHub repository.
4. Produce deployment configuration and prove a repeatable deployment of the
   baseline when the required external action is separately authorized.
5. Leave M2 and M3 with explicit, consistent foundation contracts rather than
   unresolved implementation choices.

## Non-Goals

- Building the finished homepage, professional content, CV workflow, scheduling,
  chatbot, retrieval system, or evidence corpus.
- Purchasing or configuring `panchew.io`, changing DNS or certificates, or
  performing provider or production mutations without separate authorization.
- Adding accounts, payments, analytics, behavioral tracking, uncurated evidence
  ingestion, or unauthorized personal-data inference.
- Upgrading or modifying the pinned `.governance/` dependency.
- Importing Attempt 1 commits or treating rejected decisions as accepted.
- Creating `develop`, rewriting history, or creating another recovery Epic.

## In Scope

- Fresh decisions for application framework and language, application
  architecture, deployment platform, data services, LLM-provider foundation
  constraints, repository hosting, and the production-domain path.
- A minimal application shell, public-safe health/revision behavior, local
  development and build commands, and proportionate automated checks.
- Measurable baseline accessibility, correctness, security, and performance
  budgets needed by later Milestones.
- Deployment configuration, secrets boundaries, operator authentication
  requirements, rollback/recovery instructions, and verification checks.
- Verification and documentation of the existing private GitHub `origin`, branch
  hierarchy, protected delivery workflow, and archive preservation.
- A selected apex and `www` DNS, redirect, TLS, and verification path documented
  without assuming that the domain or provider state exists.

- M2 public-experience, CV, and scheduling implementation.
- M3 LLM calls, chat UI, retrieval, citations, and evidence processing.
- Production content, final visual polish, or declaration of the public alpha.
- Domain, DNS, certificate, credential, provider, deployment, repository-setting,
  or branch-protection mutation unless Layer 8 separately authorizes the exact
  action before it occurs.

## Planned Epics

### P1-M1-E1.1 - Foundation Decisions and Working Baseline

Freshly select and record:

- Application framework and language.
- Application architecture.
- Data services and application-persistence boundaries.
- LLM-provider constraints that affect the foundation, while deferring all LLM,
  chat, retrieval, prompt, and provider integration behavior to M3.

must build and run locally, expose only the selected non-LLM baseline behavior,
and include proportionate tests and executable performance budgets. Its spec and
starter use the active Attempt 2 prefix `P1-M1-E1.1`; historical E1.1 material is
referenced only through the archive namespace.

### P1-M1-E1.2 - Hosting and Deployment Foundation

Freshly select and record:

- Deployment platform and runtime path.
- Repository-hosting workflow within the already established private GitHub
  repository.
- Production-domain path, including apex/`www`, redirects, TLS, verification,
  ownership, and recovery boundaries.

Then add the deployment configuration and verification needed to reproduce the
baseline deployment. E1.2 does not perform a real provider deployment. After E1.2
is reviewed, accepted, merged, and closed, HQ may request a standard CFO
Deployment Authorization for deployment from the accepted commit. Without that
authorization or required access, M1 remains incomplete. Its spec and starter use
the active Attempt 2 prefix `P1-M1-E1.2`.

No other M1 Epic may be planned without explicit Layer-8 approval of a different
decomposition.

## Decision Gates

- E1.1 must commit its four decisions before dependent baseline implementation.
- E1.2 must commit its three decisions before dependent deployment or hosting
  configuration.
- Each decision must be standalone, cite current primary evidence for material
  claims, define prerequisites and owners, and state concrete effects on the
  other M1 Epic and on downstream M2/M3 work.
- Architecture and LLM constraints must permit selected non-LLM baseline routes

- Performance requirements must identify reproducible tools, environments,
  metrics, thresholds, and failure behavior for local and deployed checks.
- Correctness, accessibility, and security checks must identify their tools,

- Domain and deployment decisions must fail closed when external account, plan,
  domain, DNS, certificate, or credential state is unknown.

  public portfolio evidence.
- Provide a downloadable CV.
- Provide embedded or API-based Google Calendar scheduling.

- Use curated CV content, public GitHub repositories, and commit history where

# Artifact Communication Protocol (P4.1)

## Purpose

This document defines the canonical artifact formats and communication rules for structured, predictable handoffs between governance chats in the AI Project System.

**Problem Solved:** Manual mode previously required human copy-paste between chats, creating transcription errors and breaking audit trails. Agentic mode had no standard for parent-child artifact exchange. (Transport itself is now solved better still by committed files passed by reference — AI-OPERATING-GUIDELINES.md §3.1.1; see §Integration with Manual Mode.)

**Solution:** Two canonical artifacts for the standard Epic/Milestone/Phase flow — **Delivery Notice** (produced by the child at execution completion) and **Review Decision** (produced by the parent, exception path only) — with standardized frontmatter (YAML) + markdown body. Every chat produces these when appropriate, and parent chats consume them for decisions. The Bugfix Workflow retains its own, separate two-artifact model (see §3) as a deliberate exception.

**Benefit:** 
- Automation-ready: chats can parse YAML frontmatter programmatically
- Human-readable: markdown body explains context
- Audit trail: every handoff is recorded
- No transcription: artifacts flow directly between chats
- CFO-friendly: Layer-8 sees predictable completion/review/delivery artifacts from all projects

---

## Core Principles

1. **Artifact-First Communication** — Every chat-to-chat handoff uses one of the canonical artifacts
2. **Frontmatter + Body** — YAML frontmatter for machine parsing, markdown body for human context
3. **Reference Integrity** — Every artifact includes parent_id, child_id, epic_id, milestone_id, phase_id as appropriate
4. **One Way Per Direction** — Delivery Notice flows up at execution completion; a Review Decision flows down only on the exception path (a clean delivery is accepted by silence — PSG §11.6 / AOG §12)
5. **Immutability** — Once an artifact is created, it is archived; modifications create a new versioned artifact
6. **Terminal States** — A chat declares completion via its Delivery Notice, the parent accepts a clean delivery by silence (merge + in-chat acknowledgment) and rejects or accepts-with-follow-ups via artifact on the exception path (PSG §11.6); no further artifact is produced in the standard flow after merge

									Islands architecture
									

								
	
									
	
										
Astro helped pioneer and popularize a new frontend architecture pattern called Islands Architecture. Islands architecture works by rendering the majority of your page to fast, static HTML with smaller “islands” of JavaScript added when interactivity or personalization is needed on the page (an image carousel, for example). This avoids the monolithic JavaScript payloads that slow down the responsiveness of many other, modern JavaScript web frameworks.
A brief historySection titled “A brief history”
The term “component island” was first coined by Etsy’s frontend architect Katie Sylor-Miller in 2019. This idea was then expanded on and documented in this post by Preact creator Jason Miller on August 11, 2020.

The general idea of an “Islands” architecture is deceptively simple: render HTML pages on the server, and inject placeholders or slots around highly dynamic regions […] that can then be “hydrated” on the client into small self-contained widgets, reusing their server-rendered initial HTML.
— Jason Miller, Creator of Preact

The technique that this architectural pattern builds on is also known as partial or selective hydration.
In contrast, most JavaScript-based web frameworks hydrate & render an entire website as one large JavaScript application (also known as a single-page application, or SPA). SPAs provide simplicity and power but suffer from page-load performance problems due to heavy client-side JavaScript usage.
SPAs have their place, even embedded inside an Astro page. But, SPAs lack the native ability to selectively and strategically hydrate, making them a heavy-handed choice for most projects on the web today.
Astro became popular as the first mainstream JavaScript web framework with selective hydration built-in, using that same component islands pattern first coined by Sylor-Miller. We’ve since expanded and evolved on Sylor-Miller’s original work, which helped to inspire a similar component island approach to dynamically server-rendered content.
What is an island?Section titled “What is an island?”
In Astro, an island is an enhanced UI component on an otherwise static page of HTML.
A client island is an interactive JavaScript UI component that is hydrated separately from the rest of the page, while a server island is a UI component that server-renders its dynamic content separately from the rest of the page.
Both islands run expensive or slower processes independently, on a per-component basis, for optimized page loads.
Island componentsSection titled “Island components”
Astro components are the building blocks of your page template. They render to static HTML with no client-side runtime.
Think of a client island as an interactive widget floating in a sea of otherwise static, lightweight, server-rendered HTML. Server islands can be added for personalized or dynamic server-rendered elements, such as a logged in visitor’s profile picture.

	Header (interactive island)
	Sidebar (static HTML)
	Static content like text, images, etc.
	Image carousel (interactive island)
	Footer (static HTML)

# D1 — Application Framework and Language

## Decision

`panchew-io` is implemented as a **TypeScript** application built with the
**Astro** web framework, running on the **Node.js** runtime and rendered
on demand by a Node HTTP server.

| Element | Selected value | Pin mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Language | TypeScript (as authored in `.ts` and `.astro` files, compiled by the framework's bundler) | Framework-bundled; no separate compiler in the runtime path |
| Runtime | Node.js `24.20.0` (Active LTS line "Krypton") | `.nvmrc` (exact version) + `package.json` `engines.node` (exact) + `.npmrc` `engine-strict=true` |
| Package manager | npm `11.19.0` (bundled with Node.js 24.20.0) | `package.json` `engines.npm` + the bundled-with-runtime relationship |
| Web framework | Astro `7.3.1` | Exact (non-range) version in `package.json` + `package-lock.json` (`lockfileVersion: 3`) |
| Server adapter | `@astrojs/node` `11.1.5`, `mode: 'standalone'` | Exact version in `package.json` + `package-lock.json` |
| Dependency resolution | `npm ci` against the committed `package-lock.json` | Lockfile-driven, non-mutating install |

Every direct dependency and devDependency is declared as an **exact** version
(no `^`, `~`, or other range operator), enforced by `save-exact=true` in
`.npmrc`, and resolved through the committed `package-lock.json`.

## Context and Requirements This Must Satisfy

The binding P1 constraints inherited by M2 and M3 (Project Brief §Constraints,
§Visual Success) are:

1. Fast first paint.
2. Accessible focus states.
3. Keyboard-operable surfaces, including a keyboard-operable chat (M3).
4. Strong mobile behaviour, mobile-first and predominantly single-column.
5. Reproducibility from a clean checkout with no version drift on reinstall.

M2 adds a content-heavy public experience (professional content, portfolio
evidence, a downloadable CV, an embedded or API-based scheduling surface). M3
adds a single interactive, streaming chat surface that must call a hosted LLM
API using a **server-side** secret (see D4). The application is therefore
overwhelmingly static content with a small number of genuinely interactive
regions and a small number of server endpoints.

## Options Considered

| Option | Fit against the constraints above | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Astro + Node adapter (selected)** | Renders to HTML with **no client-side runtime by default**; interactivity is added per component ("islands"), so the M3 chat widget can hydrate without shipping a framework runtime to the CV or homepage. First-class server endpoints give the M3 server-side secret boundary. | **Selected** |
| Next.js (React) | Mature and widely deployed, but React is hydrated as the default posture and the baseline client payload is materially larger for a site that is mostly static prose. Buys SPA capability the product does not need. | Rejected — pays a first-paint cost for capability M2/M3 do not require |
| SvelteKit | Comparable first-paint characteristics and a smaller runtime than React, but is component-app-first rather than content-first; content collections, Markdown/MDX authoring and per-component hydration control are less central. | Rejected — weaker fit for a content-dominant site |
| Fastify (or bare Node `http`) + hand-written templates | Minimal dependency surface and excellent raw throughput, and fully sufficient for the M1 baseline itself. Provides no view layer, no content pipeline, and no scoped styling, so the M2 "expensive consultancy finish" work would be hand-rolled HTML strings. | Rejected — optimises the M1 baseline at M2/M3's expense |
| Static-only generator (no server runtime) | Cannot hold the M3 server-side LLM secret or stream a chat response without a separate service. | Rejected — conflicts with D4 |

D1 selects the framework for **both** the baseline and the M2/M3 experience
(per the Epic spec §D1), so the M2/M3 fit is the deciding factor, not the
minimality of the M1 baseline.

## Rationale Against Each Requirement

**Fast first paint.** Astro's documented architecture renders "the majority of
your page to fast, static HTML with smaller 'islands' of JavaScript added when
interactivity or personalization is needed on the page … This avoids the
monolithic JavaScript payloads that slow down the responsiveness of many other,
modern JavaScript web frameworks" (Astro, *Islands architecture*). Astro
components "render to static HTML with no client-side runtime" (same source).
The M1 baseline ships **zero** bytes of client JavaScript.

**Accessible focus states and keyboard operability.** These are properties of
the emitted HTML and CSS, not of the framework. Astro's zero-runtime default
means the baseline and the M2 content surfaces are plain semantic HTML with
native focus behaviour, which is the lowest-risk substrate for WCAG 2.2 AA. The
framework does not intercept, virtualise, or re-implement focus. Compliance is
verified executably rather than asserted — see the accessibility check in this
Epic (`check:a11y`, axe-core over the served document).

**Strong mobile behaviour.** Delivered by CSS and by shipping less JavaScript;
the islands model is what makes "one interactive region on an otherwise static
page" achievable without a global hydration cost.

**Reproducibility.** `npm ci` "is similar to `npm install`, except it's meant to
be used in automated environments such as test platforms, continuous
integration, and deployment — or any situation where you want to make sure
you're doing a clean install of your dependencies"; it requires an existing
`package-lock.json` and "will exit with an error, instead of updating the
package lock" if the lockfile and `package.json` disagree (npm CLI v11 docs,
`npm ci`). Combined with exact version specifiers, `.nvmrc`, and
`engines` + `engine-strict=true`, a clean checkout resolves an identical
dependency graph on every install.

**Runtime version choice.** The Node.js release schedule (nodejs/Release
`schedule.json`) records:

- `v24` "Krypton" — Active LTS since `2025-10-28`, entering maintenance
  `2026-10-20`, end-of-life `2028-04-30`.
- `v22` "Jod" — in **maintenance** since `2025-10-21`, end-of-life `2027-04-30`.
- `v20` "Iron" — end-of-life `2026-04-30` (already past).

At the date of this decision, `v24` is the only line that is both LTS and not
yet in maintenance, and it carries the longest security-support horizon
(`2028-04-30`). `24.20.0` is the newest release on that line
(published `2026-08-26`, `lts: "Krypton"` in `https://nodejs.org/dist/index.json`).
Astro `7.3.1` declares `engines.node: ">=22.12.0"` and `engines.npm: ">=9.6.5"`,
so `24.20.0` / npm `11.19.0` are inside the supported range.

**Supply-chain posture.** npm 11 blocks dependency install scripts by default:
"Dependency install scripts are blocked by default. Install commands silently
skip lifecycle scripts for any dependency that does not have a matching entry in
`allowScripts`" (`npm help install-scripts`, npm 11.19.0). The project keeps that
default and records any deliberate exception in `package.json` `allowScripts`,
so a transitive package cannot execute arbitrary code at install time without an
explicit, reviewable, version-pinned entry.

## Prerequisites

- Node.js `24.20.0` and its bundled npm `11.19.0` available on the machine
  (installed via any Node version manager honouring `.nvmrc`, or from the
  official Node.js distribution; release artefacts are verifiable against the
  published `SHASUMS256.txt`).
- Network access to the npm registry for the initial `npm ci`.
- No other runtime, language toolchain, or global package is required.

## Effects on P1-M1-E1.2 (hosting and deployment)

E1.2 owns the platform decision. D1 constrains it as follows and E1.2 must
consume these as given:

1. **The deployment target must be a serverful Node.js runtime**, not a
   static-file host. `@astrojs/node` in `standalone` mode produces a Node HTTP
   server; the build output is `dist/server/entry.mjs` (server entry) plus
   `dist/client/` (static assets), started with
   `node ./dist/server/entry.mjs`.
2. **Required runtime version:** Node.js `24.x`, specifically `24.20.0`. E1.2
   must confirm the candidate platform offers that line, or record an explicit
   deviation.
3. **Build shape:** `npm ci` → `npm run build` → `npm start`. The build is
   deterministic from the lockfile and requires no platform-specific step.
4. **Configuration surface:** `HOST` and `PORT` environment variables are the
   only runtime configuration the baseline reads (both optional, with local
   defaults). E1.2 must not assume any other variable exists.
5. **Adapter portability:** if E1.2 selects a platform with its own Astro
   adapter (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare), swapping `@astrojs/node` for that
   adapter is an `astro.config.mjs` change and a new decision record — it does
   **not** invalidate D1's language/framework selection. Cloudflare-class
   (non-Node) runtimes additionally require re-verifying D4's secret boundary.
6. **No build-time secret** is required or permitted (see D4).

## Effects on M2

- M2 authors experience routes as `.astro` pages and components under
  `src/pages/` and `src/components/`, and long-form professional/CV content as
  Markdown/MDX in Astro content collections. No re-platforming is required.
- M2 inherits the "zero client JavaScript unless a component explicitly opts
  in" posture. Any interactive component must be an explicit island.
- M2 inherits the executable accessibility and performance budgets established
  by this Epic; they are floors, not targets.

## Effects on M3

- M3 implements the chat UI as a single client island and the provider call as
  a server endpoint under `src/pages/api/`, so the LLM secret never enters a
  client bundle (see D4).
- Streaming responses are available through the Node adapter's standard
  `Response` streaming; no additional framework or service is needed.
- M3 must not convert the application to a client-rendered SPA.

## Boundaries

- This decision fixes language, runtime, framework, and pinning method **only**.
  It does not select a hosting platform, a data service, or an LLM vendor.
- Changing the runtime major line, the framework, or the pinning mechanism
  requires a new decision record (PSG §10); this record is immutable once
  accepted.
- Version bumps **within** the pinned scheme (for example Node `24.20.0` →
  `24.21.0`, or a patch release of Astro) are ordinary maintenance and do not
  require a new decision, provided `.nvmrc`, `engines`, and the lockfile are
  updated together and all Epic checks still pass.

## Evidence

All sources retrieved 2026-09-07 (UTC). All are primary — the maintainer's own
documentation, release metadata, or the shipped package manifest.

| # | Claim | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E1 | Node.js `v24` "Krypton" is Active LTS from 2025-10-28, maintenance from 2026-10-20, EOL 2028-04-30; `v22` "Jod" is in maintenance from 2025-10-21, EOL 2027-04-30; `v20` "Iron" EOL 2026-04-30 | Node.js Release Working Group, `schedule.json` — <https://github.com/nodejs/Release/blob/main/schedule.json> |
| E2 | `v24.20.0` (2026-08-26) is the newest release on the v24 line and is tagged `lts: "Krypton"` | Node.js official distribution index — <https://nodejs.org/dist/index.json> |
| E3 | Node.js release artefacts are integrity-verifiable; the `node-v24.20.0-linux-x64.tar.xz` SHA-256 used for this Epic's verification runs matched the published checksum | <https://nodejs.org/dist/v24.20.0/SHASUMS256.txt> |
| E4 | Astro renders pages to static HTML with islands of JavaScript only where interactivity is needed; "Astro components … render to static HTML with no client-side runtime" | Astro Docs, *Islands architecture* — <https://docs.astro.build/en/concepts/islands/> |
| E5 | Astro `7.3.1` is the current published release and declares `engines.node: ">=22.12.0"`, `engines.npm: ">=9.6.5"` | npm registry metadata for `astro` and the installed `node_modules/astro/package.json` |
| E6 | `@astrojs/node` `11.1.5` is the current published Node adapter; `standalone` mode emits a runnable Node HTTP server | npm registry metadata; Astro Docs, *Node adapter* — <https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/node/> |
| E7 | `npm ci` is intended for automated/clean installs, requires an existing lockfile, and errors rather than updating the lockfile on mismatch | npm CLI v11 Docs, `npm ci` — <https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npm-ci> |
| E8 | npm 11 blocks dependency install scripts by default and records approvals in `package.json` `allowScripts` | `npm help install-scripts`, npm `11.19.0` (shipped man page) |
| E9 | Astro documents Vitest for unit/integration testing and Playwright for end-to-end testing | Astro Docs, *Testing* — <https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/testing/> |

## Verification Performed

The selection was verified, not assumed, before this record was accepted as the
basis for code:

- Node.js `24.20.0` was downloaded, checksum-verified against `SHASUMS256.txt`,
  and executed (`node -v` → `v24.20.0`, `npm -v` → `11.19.0`).
- An Astro `7.3.1` + `@astrojs/node` `11.1.5` project was installed, built, and
  started on that runtime, confirming: a JSON endpoint returning
  `content-type: application/json`, an HTML page returning
  `content-type: text/html`, a `404` for an unmatched route, no
  `X-Powered-By`-style disclosure header, and no filesystem path in any response.
- `npm audit` over the resulting dependency graph reported `found 0
  vulnerabilities`.

## Related

- D2 — Application architecture (consumes the framework and adapter chosen here)
- D3 — Data services and application-persistence boundaries
- D4 — LLM-provider foundation constraints
- [Epic P1-M1-E1.1 spec](../phases/P1__Alpha_Platform_Launch/P1-M1-E1.1__spec__foundation-decisions-and-working-baseline.md)

phase: P1
milestone: M1

type: decision
status: active
last_updated: 2026-09-07

title: Application architecture
owner: Epic P1-M1-E1.1 executor, on behalf of the project owner (Layer 8)

# D2 — Application Architecture

## Decision

`panchew-io` is a **single, server-rendered, file-routed Astro application with
selective client hydration (islands)**, served by one long-lived Node HTTP
process. There is no separate front-end application, no client-side router, and
no additional back-end service.

Concretely:

1. **Rendering model.** On-demand server rendering for every route
   (`output: 'server'` in `astro.config.mjs`), served by `@astrojs/node` in
   `standalone` mode. HTML is generated per request on the server.
2. **Client-side JavaScript.** None by default. A component ships JavaScript
   only by being declared an island with an explicit `client:*` directive. The
   M1 baseline ships **zero** client JavaScript and has **zero** island
   components.
3. **Routing surface.** File-based routing under `src/pages/`. A file at
   `src/pages/<name>.astro` serves the HTML route `/<name>`; a file at
   `src/pages/<name>.ts` exporting a `GET` handler serves a non-HTML endpoint at
   `/<name>`. Any request that matches no file returns `404` from the adapter.
4. **Component boundaries.** Four directories, each with one responsibility:

   | Directory | Responsibility | Present in M1 |
   | --- | --- | --- |
   | `src/pages/` | Routes only. HTML pages (`.astro`) and endpoints (`.ts`). No business logic. | Yes — exactly three route files |
   | `src/layouts/` | Shared document shell (`<html>`, `<head>`, landmarks, global styles). | Deferred to M2 (the M1 page is a single self-contained document) |
   | `src/components/` | Presentational components and, later, client islands. | Deferred to M2 |
   | `src/lib/` | Framework-independent server-side logic and constants. Never imported by a client island. | Yes — `src/lib/revision.ts` |

5. **Build output shape.** `npm run build` emits `dist/server/entry.mjs` (the
   server entry) and `dist/client/` (static assets). `npm start` runs
   `node ./dist/server/entry.mjs`. Nothing else is required at runtime.
6. **Runtime configuration.** Exactly two optional environment variables,
   `HOST` and `PORT`, both read by the adapter. No other environment input is
   read by M1 code.

## The M1 Route Surface Is Closed

The **only** routes that exist in M1 are:

| Route | Status | Content type | Body |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /health` | `200` | `application/json` | `{"status":"ok"}` |
| `GET /revision` | `200` | `application/json` | `{"revision":"<public-safe label>"}` |
| `GET /` | `200` | `text/html` | Minimal accessible status document |
| anything else | `404` | — | — |

This is enforced structurally: `src/pages/` contains exactly three files, and
Astro's file-based routing means a route cannot exist without a corresponding
file. It is enforced executably by the correctness suite, which asserts each of
the three routes and asserts `404` for unmatched paths.

The `GET /` document is a **status page**, not the M2 homepage. Its visible text
is limited to its own title and the revision label. It exists to prove that the
stack renders accessible HTML, and M2 replaces it.

## Prohibition of M3 Behaviour in M1 and M2

**No LLM, chat, retrieval, prompt, embedding, vector, or provider-integration
behaviour may exist in M1 or M2.** This is an architectural rule, not a
scheduling preference:

- No module under `src/` may import an LLM SDK or issue an outbound HTTP request
  to a model provider before M3.
- No route in M1 or M2 may proxy, forward, or relay a request to any external
  inference service.
- The M1 baseline performs **zero outbound network calls** while serving
  requests. This is a measurable property and is relied upon by the performance
  budget, which is defined as local-only and network-free.

See D4 for the secret and network boundary that backs this prohibition.

## Where M2 and M3 Attach

The architecture is chosen so that later work is **additive**. No foundation
change is required for either Milestone.

### M2 — public experience

| M2 concern | Attachment point | Foundation change required |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Homepage (replaces the M1 status page) | `src/pages/index.astro` | None |
| Professional content / portfolio pages | new `src/pages/*.astro` | None |
| Shared document shell, header, footer | new `src/layouts/Base.astro`, adopted by pages | None |
| Long-form CV / portfolio content | Astro content collections under `src/content/` | None |
| Downloadable CV asset | `public/` (served as a static asset by `dist/client/`) | None |
| Scheduling surface (embed or API-based) | `src/components/` island for the widget; `src/pages/api/*.ts` if a server-side call is required | None |
| Site-wide headers / caching / redirects | `src/middleware.ts` (Astro middleware) — not present in M1 | None |

M2 **must not** delete or repurpose `/health` or `/revision`; they are the
operational contract E1.2's deployment verification depends on.

### M3 — evidence-citing chatbot

| M3 concern | Attachment point | Foundation change required |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chat UI (streaming, keyboard-operable) | a single client island in `src/components/`, hydrated on the page that hosts it | None |
| Provider call (server-side, secret-bearing) | `src/pages/api/chat.ts` — a server endpoint returning a streamed `Response` | None |
| Provider client, prompt assembly, citation logic | `src/lib/llm/**` — server-only, never imported by an island | None |
| Retrieval / evidence index access | `src/lib/retrieval/**`, consuming the persistence boundary defined in D3 | None (D3 governs the store itself) |

`src/pages/api/` and `src/lib/llm/` are **reserved namespaces**: they do not
exist in M1, must not be created in M2 for LLM purposes, and are the only places
an LLM provider call may originate.

## Rationale

- **One process, one deployable.** A single Node server that renders HTML and
  serves the handful of endpoints the product needs is the smallest architecture
  that satisfies M1, M2, and M3. Splitting the chat backend into a second
  service would add a deployment target, a network hop on the latency-critical
  chat path, and a cross-service auth boundary, for no benefit at this scale.
- **Server rendering, not static generation.** A purely static build cannot hold
  the M3 server-side secret or stream a provider response (D4). Choosing
  `output: 'server'` at M1 avoids a rendering-model migration between M2 and M3.
- **Islands, not global hydration.** The product is content with one interactive
  region. Islands let the CV and homepage ship no JavaScript while the chat
  widget is fully interactive: "an island is an enhanced UI component on an
  otherwise static page of HTML … hydrated separately from the rest of the page"
  (Astro, *Islands architecture*).
- **File-based routing as the enforcement mechanism.** Because a route requires a
  file, the closed M1 route surface is auditable by listing one directory rather
  than by reading a router configuration.
- **Deferring layouts, components, and middleware is deliberate.** Creating empty
  scaffolding directories in M1 would be unproven structure. The table above
  names their contract so M2 does not have to re-decide it.

## Prerequisites

- D1 (Astro `7.3.1`, `@astrojs/node` `11.1.5`, Node.js `24.20.0`) — this
  decision is expressed entirely in terms of that stack.
- No external service, data store, or credential.

## Effects on P1-M1-E1.2 (hosting and deployment)

1. **The platform must run a long-lived Node HTTP server** and route **all**
   paths to it — including unmatched paths, so that the application (not the
   platform) produces the `404`. A static-file host is not viable.
2. **The platform must supply `PORT`** (and may supply `HOST`); the adapter
   binds to them. No other configuration is needed to start.
3. **`GET /health` is the deployment health check.** It is dependency-free,
   performs no outbound call, and returns `200` with `{"status":"ok"}`. E1.2
   should configure it as the platform readiness/liveness probe.
4. **`GET /revision` is the deployment verification endpoint.** After a
   deployment, comparing its `revision` value against the deployed commit proves
   which build is live. E1.2's verification procedure should use it.
5. **Cold start is a platform selection criterion.** The baseline's measured
   cold start is recorded in this Epic's Delivery Notice; a platform that
   suspends idle instances must keep the observed cold start within the
   `≤ 10 s` budget this Epic establishes.
6. **No build-time or runtime secret is required** to deploy the M1 baseline.

## Effects on M2

- M2 adds files; it does not restructure. Every M2 surface has a named
  attachment point above.
- M2 must preserve `/health` and `/revision` exactly as specified.
- M2 must keep the default zero-JavaScript posture: any interactivity is an
  explicit, justified island.
- M2 introduces no LLM behaviour of any kind.

## Effects on M3

- M3's provider call is confined to `src/pages/api/**` and `src/lib/llm/**`.
- M3's chat UI is one island; the rest of the page remains static HTML.
- M3 requires no change to the rendering model, the adapter, or the build shape.

## Boundaries

- This decision fixes the architecture only. It does not select a hosting
  platform (E1.2), a data store (D3), or an LLM vendor (D4).
- Adding a second deployable service, a client-side router, an SPA shell, or a
  build-time-only (static) output mode would each require a new decision record.

## Evidence

All sources retrieved 2026-09-07 (UTC).

| # | Claim | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E1 | Astro islands: static HTML by default with selectively hydrated interactive components; Astro components render with no client-side runtime | Astro Docs, *Islands architecture* — <https://docs.astro.build/en/concepts/islands/> |
| E2 | `output: 'server'` enables on-demand server rendering for all routes and requires an adapter | Astro Docs, *On-demand rendering* — <https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/on-demand-rendering/> |
| E3 | `@astrojs/node` `standalone` mode produces a runnable Node HTTP server that binds `HOST`/`PORT` | Astro Docs, *Node adapter* — <https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/node/> |
| E4 | File-based routing: files in `src/pages/` become routes; unmatched requests produce a 404 | Astro Docs, *Routing* — <https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/routing/> |
| E5 | Endpoints: a `.ts` file in `src/pages/` exporting `GET` serves non-HTML responses via the standard `Response` API | Astro Docs, *Endpoints* — <https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/endpoints/> |
| E6 | Astro middleware (`src/middleware.ts`) is the documented interception point for cross-cutting request handling | Astro Docs, *Middleware* — <https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/middleware/> |

## Verification Performed

On the D1 stack, before this record was accepted as the basis for code:

- A three-file `src/pages/` project served `application/json` from a `.ts`
  endpoint and `text/html` from an `.astro` page, and returned `404` for an
  unmatched path — with no route configuration beyond the files themselves.
- The build emitted `dist/server/entry.mjs` + `dist/client/`, and
  `node ./dist/server/entry.mjs` served all routes.
- Responses carried no framework disclosure header and no filesystem path.
